$comment: What yonto.fetch refuses to send, and what it changes before sending, on both hosts. The rules are the WHATWG Fetch standard's (https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/): its forbidden methods, its method normalisation, its forbidden request-headers, its refusal of a URL carrying credentials and of a GET or HEAD with a body, and the Content-Type it gives a string body. Three forbidden request-headers are let through, each for the reason in `allowedDespiteFetch`, and a header value must be printable ASCII or a tab, which is stricter than Fetch because OkHttp cannot send anything else. A refusal is REQUEST_INVALID, and nothing is sent. The CLI reads this file (src/host/request-shape.js); the device keeps the same lists in PluginRequestShape, held to this file by PluginRequestRulesRecordTest. Both walk every entry of every list, and every case below, through their own yonto.fetch (test/request-rules.test.js on the CLI). A case either names the refusal or what was sent: the method, and the Content-Type header when the case says one. `redirectsTo` makes the first answer a 302 there.

allowedDespiteFetch.cookie: Fetch forbids it so a page cannot forge the browser's cookie jar. A plugin has no jar to forge: the host attaches a cookieLogin session over whatever Cookie the plugin set (see the contract), and XPTV catalogs send back a cookie a site handed them (plugins/xptv-js, bdys.js).
allowedDespiteFetch.origin: Fetch forbids it because the browser, not the page, knows which page a request came from. A plugin is no page, and sites check it as they check Referer: two of the three recorded XPTV catalogs send it (plugins/xptv-js/fixtures/catalogs, ddys.js and tianyiso.js).
allowedDespiteFetch.referer: The same reason as Origin, and shipped plugins send it: plugins/ddys, and every recorded XPTV catalog through plugins/xptv-js.
